mcqs.question: Why is computing diameter as just "the sum of the two subtree heights at the root" wrong for many trees?
options: Height cannot be computed recursively
Diameter is always equal to the tree's total node count
The longest path in a tree doesn't need to pass through the root at all — it could lie entirely within one subtree, so the true diameter requires checking every node, not just the root
This formula only works for trees with an odd number of nodes
mcqs.explanation: The longest path between any two nodes can be located entirely within a single subtree, off to one side, never touching the root — so restricting the check to the root alone misses those cases. Diameter and node count are unrelated in general, height is naturally computed recursively, and node-count parity has no bearing on this.

mcqs.question: Why does calling a separate `height()` function from inside a diameter recursion turn an O(n) algorithm into O(n²)?
options: It doesn't — both versions have the same time complexity
Each call re-walks and recomputes subtree heights that a combined single-pass function would have already computed, repeating that work at every node in the recursion
It only becomes slower when the tree contains duplicate values
Separate function calls are always O(n) regardless of what they compute
mcqs.explanation: Recomputing a subtree's height from scratch at every ancestor node redundantly repeats work that a single combined post-order pass would have already produced once — that repetition across all nodes is exactly what degrades the complexity to O(n²) in the worst case. This is a genuine complexity difference between the two approaches, unrelated to duplicate values, and calling a separate function doesn't guarantee O(n) on its own — it depends on what that function recomputes.

mcqs.question: In the max path sum solution, why does each child's contribution get clamped with `max(helper(child), 0)` before being used?
options: To ensure the algorithm runs in O(log n) instead of O(n)
To handle trees that contain no negative values
To convert the tree into a valid BST before computing path sums
A negative-sum subtree should be excluded from the path entirely rather than dragging the total down, and clamping to 0 achieves exactly that
mcqs.explanation: If including a child's best path would only lower the total, the optimal choice is to simply not extend the path into that subtree — treating a negative contribution as 0 achieves precisely that without needing a separate branch of logic. This doesn't affect the algorithm's time complexity, it's specifically needed because negative values can appear, and it has nothing to do with BST validity.

mcqs.question: Why is it incorrect for the max-path-sum helper function to return a value that includes both the left and right child contributions?
options: A path can only pass through a given node once without branching, so a value using both children represents an already-bent path that can't be validly extended further upward by the parent
Returning both contributions makes the function run slower
This is actually correct and is the standard implementation
Left and right subtree values cannot be added together in this context
mcqs.explanation: A valid path visits each node once and doesn't branch, so a node using both its children to form a path has already reached that path's turning point — passing that combined value up as if the parent could extend it further would imply a second bend, producing an invalid, over-counted path. This is a correctness issue, not a performance one, and it's specifically the bug to avoid, not the correct implementation.

mcqs.question: A problem asks whether any root-to-leaf path sums to a target value. Does this need the "return one value, track another" diameter-style pattern?
options: No — since the path is anchored at the root and must end at a leaf, a straightforward top-down recursion checking the remaining target suffices, with no separate tracked value needed
Yes — every tree path-sum problem requires this pattern
No — this problem can only be solved with a hash map, no recursion
Yes, but only if the tree is a valid BST
mcqs.explanation: The return-one-track-another pattern exists specifically for paths that can start and end anywhere, making every node a potential turning point; a root-to-leaf-anchored path has no such ambiguity, so a simple recursion subtracting values along the way and checking for zero at a leaf is sufficient. Not every path-sum variant needs the complex pattern, this problem doesn't require a hash map, and it applies to any binary tree, not just BSTs.

mcqs.question: A problem asks for the count of downward paths (not necessarily root-to-leaf) summing to a target. Which pattern fits best, and why not the diameter-style pattern?
options: The diameter-style pattern, since all tree path problems use the identical technique
A prefix-sum-with-backtracking approach, since the goal is a count of paths rather than an extreme value, and paths are constrained to go strictly downward, which prefix sums track naturally
Neither pattern applies — this problem cannot be solved with a single traversal
The diameter-style pattern, because it's the only technique that tracks a value separately from the return value
mcqs.explanation: The distinguishing features here are 'count, not max' and 'strictly downward, not free-floating' — exactly the shape prefix-sum-with-backtracking is built for, using ancestor prefix sums to count valid path starts rather than tracking an extreme value across arbitrary node pairs. Not all tree path problems share one universal technique, this problem is solvable in a single DFS pass, and separate-value-tracking isn't unique to the diameter pattern — prefix-sum tracking also tracks state separately from its return value, just for a different purpose.
